description.text: The right humerus is the long bone of the arm between the shoulder and elbow. Its expanded ends provide joint surfaces, while its shaft supplies extensive muscle and fascial attachments. The proximal end consists of a rounded head and adjacent tubercles; the distal end widens into the elbow condyle and epicondyles. These regions must be distinguished from the shaft when assessing orientation or an injury.

The head faces medially, superiorly and somewhat posteriorly toward the glenoid. The lesser tubercle is anterior; the greater tubercle is lateral. The large olecranon fossa is posterior at the distal end. Taken together, these features establish anatomical orientation; apparent screen left or right alone does not establish bone laterality.

The shaft changes from a more rounded proximal profile to a triangular distal profile. Three surfaces and three borders organize its muscle attachments. Distally, the articular trochlea is medial to the capitulum; the epicondyles are non-articular projections flanking this joint surface. Fossae above the articular region accommodate the forearm bones during elbow movement.

classification.text: Long bone of the appendicular skeleton. A compact-walled shaft surrounds the medullary canal, while the expanded ends contain cancellous bone beneath a cortical covering.

location.text: The right arm lies distal to the pectoral girdle and proximal to the forearm. The humeral head meets the scapula; the distal condyle meets the radius and ulna.

structureAndFunction.text: The bone acts as a lever for shoulder and elbow movements and anchors muscles acting on the shoulder, elbow, forearm and wrist. Its shaft separates major anterior and posterior muscle attachments; its joint surfaces transfer forces between the upper limb and the shoulder girdle.

attachments.text: At the proximal end, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor insert on the greater tubercle; subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle. Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major attach respectively to the lateral lip, floor and medial lip of the intertubercular groove.

Deltoid inserts on the deltoid tuberosity; coracobrachialis inserts medially on the shaft. Brachialis arises from the distal anterior humerus. The humeral triceps heads originate posteriorly, separated in part by the radial groove. Biceps crosses the bone without a humeral insertion.

The distal epicondylar regions provide common forearm muscle origins and elbow collateral-ligament attachments. The medial and lateral intermuscular septa attach along the corresponding distal shaft ridges, contributing to the boundaries of the arm compartments.

articulations.text: The head articulates with the scapular glenoid at the glenohumeral joint. At the elbow, the capitulum articulates with the radial head and the trochlea with the ulnar trochlear notch.

facts.text: Identify the medially directed head, anterior lesser tubercle and posterior olecranon fossa together. The left/right identity is stored in the canonical source mapping and is not inferred from camera perspective.
The proximal humerus receives circumflex humeral arterial contributions from the axillary system. Nutrient and periosteal vessels derived from brachial and profunda brachii branches supply the shaft.
The relative contributions to the humeral head are not captured by a single arterial label; injury and surgical exposure can disturb this regional vascular network.

The humerus forms by endochondral ossification: a cartilage model is progressively replaced by bone. The shaft develops before its epiphyseal regions; growth plates separate developing ends from the diaphysis during growth.

facts.text: The classical eight-centre scheme comprises the shaft, head, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, capitulum, trochlea and the two epicondyles. The olecranon belongs to the ulna and must not be counted as a humeral centre.

Gray (1918) describes fetal shaft ossification followed by separate postnatal proximal and distal centres and later fusion. Its exact appearance/fusion ages are historical observations, not validated age-estimation rules for current patients. Modern skeletal maturation varies and requires age-, sex- and population-appropriate evidence.

facts.text: A supracondylar process may project from the distal anteromedial humerus. A fibrous connection to the medial epicondyle can relate to median-nerve or brachial-artery compression. The cited dry-bone study is a sample observation, not a universal prevalence estimate.

A supratrochlear aperture is a variable opening through the septum between coronoid and olecranon fossae. It should not be confused with a normal nutrient foramen or assumed to exist in this individual source mesh.

The distal medial and lateral epicondyles provide palpable, non-articular reference points on either side of the elbow. The more proximal humerus lies beneath muscle and should be interpreted using its relationships to the shoulder and arm, not treated as uniformly subcutaneous.

attachments.text: At the proximal end, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor insert on the greater tubercle; subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle. Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major attach respectively to the lateral lip, floor and medial lip of the intertubercular groove.

Deltoid inserts on the deltoid tuberosity; coracobrachialis inserts medially on the shaft. Brachialis arises from the distal anterior humerus. The humeral triceps heads originate posteriorly, separated in part by the radial groove. Biceps crosses the bone without a humeral insertion.

The distal epicondylar regions provide common forearm muscle origins and elbow collateral-ligament attachments. The medial and lateral intermuscular septa attach along the corresponding distal shaft ridges, contributing to the boundaries of the arm compartments.

articulations.text: The head articulates with the scapular glenoid at the glenohumeral joint. At the elbow, the capitulum articulates with the radial head and the trochlea with the ulnar trochlear notch.

facts.text: Identify the medially directed head, anterior lesser tubercle and posterior olecranon fossa together. The left/right identity is stored in the canonical source mapping and is not inferred from camera perspective.
The proximal humerus receives circumflex humeral arterial contributions from the axillary system. Nutrient and periosteal vessels derived from brachial and profunda brachii branches supply the shaft.
The relative contributions to the humeral head are not captured by a single arterial label; injury and surgical exposure can disturb this regional vascular network.

The humerus forms by endochondral ossification: a cartilage model is progressively replaced by bone. The shaft develops before its epiphyseal regions; growth plates separate developing ends from the diaphysis during growth.

facts.text: The classical eight-centre scheme comprises the shaft, head, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, capitulum, trochlea and the two epicondyles. The olecranon belongs to the ulna and must not be counted as a humeral centre.

Gray (1918) describes fetal shaft ossification followed by separate postnatal proximal and distal centres and later fusion. Its exact appearance/fusion ages are historical observations, not validated age-estimation rules for current patients. Modern skeletal maturation varies and requires age-, sex- and population-appropriate evidence.

detailed.reviewNote: A consulted modern indexed overview inconsistently includes the olecranon among humeral centres. This conflict is not silently copied. Contemporary quantitative timing needs review.

facts.text: A supracondylar process may project from the distal anteromedial humerus. A fibrous connection to the medial epicondyle can relate to median-nerve or brachial-artery compression. The cited dry-bone study is a sample observation, not a universal prevalence estimate.

A supratrochlear aperture is a variable opening through the septum between coronoid and olecranon fossae. It should not be confused with a normal nutrient foramen or assumed to exist in this individual source mesh.

The distal medial and lateral epicondyles provide palpable, non-articular reference points on either side of the elbow. The more proximal humerus lies beneath muscle and should be interpreted using its relationships to the shoulder and arm, not treated as uniformly subcutaneous.

description.text: The left radius lies on the thumb side of the forearm in anatomical position. A small proximal head and neck lead into a curved shaft that expands substantially at the wrist. The bone articulates with the humerus and ulna proximally, with the ulna distally and with the carpal region.

description.text: The left ulna is the medial forearm long bone in anatomical position. Its large proximal end forms the principal bony hinge with the humeral trochlea. In contrast with the radius, the shaft narrows toward a comparatively small distal head and styloid.

The olecranon and coronoid process bound the trochlear notch. A separate radial notch on the lateral proximal end articulates with the radial head. The shaft has anterior, posterior and medial surfaces, an interosseous border facing the radius and a readily accessible posterior border. An articular disc separates the distal ulna from direct carpal articulation.

structureAndFunction.text: The proximal ulna provides elbow stability while its relationship to the radius permits forearm rotation. Muscle and membrane attachments integrate both bones rather than allowing either shaft to function in isolation.

The right humerus is the long bone of the arm between the shoulder and elbow. Its expanded ends provide joint surfaces, while its shaft supplies extensive muscle and fascial attachments. The proximal end consists of a rounded head and adjacent tubercles; the distal end widens into the elbow condyle and epicondyles. These regions must be distinguished from the shaft when assessing orientation or an injury.

The head faces medially, superiorly and somewhat posteriorly toward the glenoid. The lesser tubercle is anterior; the greater tubercle is lateral. The large olecranon fossa is posterior at the distal end. Taken together, these features establish anatomical orientation; apparent screen left or right alone does not establish bone laterality.

The shaft changes from a more rounded proximal profile to a triangular distal profile. Three surfaces and three borders organize its muscle attachments. Distally, the articular trochlea is medial to the capitulum; the epicondyles are non-articular projections flanking this joint surface. Fossae above the articular region accommodate the forearm bones during elbow movement.
Long bone of the appendicular skeleton. A compact-walled shaft surrounds the medullary canal, while the expanded ends contain cancellous bone beneath a cortical covering.
The right arm lies distal to the pectoral girdle and proximal to the forearm. The humeral head meets the scapula; the distal condyle meets the radius and ulna.

The bone acts as a lever for shoulder and elbow movements and anchors muscles acting on the shoulder, elbow, forearm and wrist. Its shaft separates major anterior and posterior muscle attachments; its joint surfaces transfer forces between the upper limb and the shoulder girdle.
The rounded proximal articular region faces the glenoid cavity. Its margin is delimited by the anatomical neck, separating the smooth head from the tubercles.
A groove bordering the head and providing attachment to the shoulder joint capsule. It is proximal to the surgical neck and should not be used as a synonym for it.
The lateral proximal prominence bears superior, middle and inferior tendon impressions for supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor respectively.
The anterior proximal prominence receives subscapularis. The intertubercular sulcus separates it from the greater tubercle.
The narrowing immediately distal to the tubercles connects the proximal expansion with the shaft. It is anatomically distinct from the rim around the head.
The shaft has three surfaces and three borders. Its proximal and distal shape differ, and the deltoid tuberosity and radial groove interrupt an otherwise continuous cortical surface.

The distal articular complex includes the capitulum laterally and trochlea medially. Adjacent fossae and epicondyles are important neighbouring features, rather than interchangeable names for these joint surfaces.
The shaft surface between the anterior and lateral borders includes the deltoid tuberosity. Distal to this attachment it contributes to the origin of brachialis.
The shaft surface between anterior and medial borders includes the continuation of the intertubercular region, a coracobrachialis insertion area and a distal brachialis origin area.
The radial groove crosses this region. The lateral head of triceps originates superior to the groove and the medial head principally inferior to it.

The boundary between the two anterior shaft surfaces descends from the greater-tubercle crest toward the coronoid fossa; it is related to pectoralis major insertion proximally and brachialis attachment distally.

The boundary between anteromedial and posterior regions extends toward the medial epicondyle. Distally it contributes to the medial supracondylar ridge and attachment of the medial intermuscular septum.
This boundary between anterolateral and posterior surfaces descends toward the lateral epicondyle, becoming the lateral supracondylar ridge distally. The radial groove crosses its middle region.
The rounded lateral distal articular prominence meets the fovea of the radial head. Its articular surface is mainly anterior and inferior.
The pulley-shaped medial distal articular surface fits the trochlear notch of the ulna and extends onto the anterior, inferior and posterior aspects of the distal bone.
The groove between the proximal tubercles accommodates the tendon of the long head of biceps. Its floor and two lips have distinct muscle attachments.
The lateral lip of the intertubercular sulcus provides insertion for pectoralis major and continues toward the anterior shaft border.
The medial lip of the intertubercular sulcus receives teres major. Latissimus dorsi attaches in the floor of the groove rather than on this crest.
A roughened lateral mid-shaft insertion area for deltoid. It provides an orientation landmark and a useful reference when describing shaft attachments.
An oblique posterior shaft groove related to the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels. Triceps origins lie on either side of this region.
The larger medial distal projection gives attachment to the common flexor origin and ulnar collateral ligament. The ulnar nerve passes behind it.
The lateral distal prominence gives attachment to the common extensor region and radial collateral ligament of the elbow.
The anterior depression above the trochlea receives the coronoid process of the ulna as the elbow flexes.
The small anterior depression above the capitulum accommodates the radial head during elbow flexion.
The large posterior distal depression accommodates the olecranon during elbow extension. A thin septum separates it from the anterior coronoid fossa.
A distal continuation of the medial border associated with the medial intermuscular septum and neighbouring muscle origins.
The distal lateral ridge gives attachment to brachioradialis superiorly, extensor carpi radialis longus inferiorly and the lateral intermuscular septum.

At the proximal end, supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor insert on the greater tubercle; subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle. Pectoralis major, latissimus dorsi and teres major attach respectively to the lateral lip, floor and medial lip of the intertubercular groove.

Deltoid inserts on the deltoid tuberosity; coracobrachialis inserts medially on the shaft. Brachialis arises from the distal anterior humerus. The humeral triceps heads originate posteriorly, separated in part by the radial groove. Biceps crosses the bone without a humeral insertion.

The distal epicondylar regions provide common forearm muscle origins and elbow collateral-ligament attachments. The medial and lateral intermuscular septa attach along the corresponding distal shaft ridges, contributing to the boundaries of the arm compartments.
The head articulates with the scapular glenoid at the glenohumeral joint. At the elbow, the capitulum articulates with the radial head and the trochlea with the ulnar trochlear notch.

Surgical-neck trauma can affect the axillary nerve, producing deltoid weakness and sensory disturbance over the lateral shoulder. A humeral-shaft lesion can affect the radial nerve and weaken wrist and finger extension. These are anatomical correlations; deficits depend on lesion level.

Shaft injuries require attention to the radial nerve and nearby profunda brachii vessels. Examination includes distal circulation and motor/sensory function, with the injury pattern and associated lesions interpreted by a qualified clinician. This atlas does not diagnose a fracture or determine treatment.

Identify the medially directed head, anterior lesser tubercle and posterior olecranon fossa together. The left/right identity is stored in the canonical source mapping and is not inferred from camera perspective.
The proximal humerus receives circumflex humeral arterial contributions from the axillary system. Nutrient and periosteal vessels derived from brachial and profunda brachii branches supply the shaft.
The relative contributions to the humeral head are not captured by a single arterial label; injury and surgical exposure can disturb this regional vascular network.

The humerus forms by endochondral ossification: a cartilage model is progressively replaced by bone. The shaft develops before its epiphyseal regions; growth plates separate developing ends from the diaphysis during growth.

The classical eight-centre scheme comprises the shaft, head, greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, capitulum, trochlea and the two epicondyles. The olecranon belongs to the ulna and must not be counted as a humeral centre.

Gray (1918) describes fetal shaft ossification followed by separate postnatal proximal and distal centres and later fusion. Its exact appearance/fusion ages are historical observations, not validated age-estimation rules for current patients. Modern skeletal maturation varies and requires age-, sex- and population-appropriate evidence.

A supracondylar process may project from the distal anteromedial humerus. A fibrous connection to the medial epicondyle can relate to median-nerve or brachial-artery compression. The cited dry-bone study is a sample observation, not a universal prevalence estimate.

A supratrochlear aperture is a variable opening through the septum between coronoid and olecranon fossae. It should not be confused with a normal nutrient foramen or assumed to exist in this individual source mesh.

The distal medial and lateral epicondyles provide palpable, non-articular reference points on either side of the elbow. The more proximal humerus lies beneath muscle and should be interpreted using its relationships to the shoulder and arm, not treated as uniformly subcutaneous.
